title: Non Abiding
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing simplicity in spiritual practice, allowing us to release our need for structures and concepts that create suffering. By letting go of dualistic thinking and perceiving reality as it truly is, we can directly experience the present moment without conceptual elaboration, revealing a simple and interconnected world where everything is empty of inherent existence. This approach requires balance, as it must be tempered with a systematic understanding of the Buddha's teachings to avoid falling into extremes.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Thank you for being here.
That was just a little aside.

I wanted to share a little more with you from a book of talks that I brought up about a month or maybe several months ago by Ajahn Amaro, who's an American-born Theravadan monk with a [unclear: "navel"] monastery in California.
He once gave a long retreat with a Tibetan teacher, and these are talks from that retreat.
I think they're particularly helpful to us because the Tibetan teacher was closer to the Zen end of Buddhism.
In his talks, he's being a little more [unclear: "expletive"] and reflecting the Theravadan, the older Buddhist tradition, against the mirror of the Mahayana, the more elaborated version of Buddhism.

So it's really clear, and helpful for us to understand as foundational, that the great wonder of Zen is that it actually does somehow work to have somebody show up out of the blue and you tell them, just sit down.
That's all the instruction.
Just sit down in the middle of your life.
There's a little technique about breathing or letting go of breathing.
But somehow, with very little instruction and very little theory or operative stuff, it actually works, because it kind of liberates us.

Because we come into everything that we do expecting there to be a manual, you know what I mean, and steps and processes and bullet points and rubrics and evaluative structures, so you can figure out if you're doing it well or badly or if you're making progress.
Zen is, in some ways, wonderfully liberated from all these things, despite what I said before about all these other ceremonies, you know what I mean?
We really don't know.
We have no idea.
Am I an advanced student or a beginning student?
I have no idea.
No clue.
Do those categories even mean anything in this context?
I don't know.
I don't understand.
And so I can therefore release that grasping mind a little more, which is actually the point of all Buddhism, to be able to release.
One Japanese Zen teacher says that Zen is opening the hand of thought.
Instead of gripping onto your thoughts, actually just open that hand.
Let your thoughts float away.

Zen is wonderful that way, but it's also problematic, because you also get people, and I met with somebody not too long ago, who get that very basic instruction, sit down, and just kind of stew for the next 20 years, you know what I mean?
It actually isn't really transformational.
It's not really helping them.
Maybe it's relaxing, or at least keeps them out of trouble for that half hour, but it's not nearly the potential of Dharma, you know what I mean?
The Theravadan guys are a little more systematic.
See what I'm saying?
So there's a counterbalance here.
The great opportunity of American Dharma is that these different schools of Buddhism are able to access each other in a way that they couldn't before.
A 16th century Japanese Zen teacher had no access to this material.
Very few of them would travel to Sri Lanka or somewhere, and then they'd have language and cultural barriers, and maybe learn something.
Now we can pick up a book in English in our library.
I'm not aware of any Theravadan activity in Japan.
I think so.
But then the different Japanese Buddhist schools are quite various too.
It wasn't just Zen.
Anyway, I wanted to read you a little bit.
This is reflections from Ajahn Amaro, thinking about his teacher, a British-born monk named Ajahn Sumedho, thinking about his teacher, a Thai teacher named Ajahn Chah.
Ajahn Chah was a very important Thai teacher, and he's a root teacher for the whole American Vipassana movement and also for a lot of the American and Western people who ended up ordaining.
The so-called older teachings of Sri Lanka and Thailand and Burma came over in three different waves to America.
I'm going to use my whole time on introductions, sorry.
But it's kind of interesting, I guess.

One wave has been a very quiet, gradual wave since probably the 30s or 40s: immigrants from those countries bringing their practices with them, bringing monks and teachers and creating community temples.
For the most part, Western America ignored that, and still does ignore it to a saddening extent, which we'll work on.
This generation will work on that.
So there's been immigrant Buddhism coming along quietly.
Then there are two different important ways American Buddhism came from these teachings.
The first wave were people like Jack Cornfield and Sharon Salzberg, a small group of mostly Jewish, actually, Americans, who found themselves in Thailand for one reason or another.
Some of them ordained for a while, some of them not.
They practiced deeply and thought to themselves, these are amazing meditation trainings.
I can't believe what I'm learning about my mind and how much it's changing me.
But our buddies back home are never going to go through all this other stuff, all this religion stuff.
So this was the American Vipassana movement.
They left almost all the religion behind and just brought meditative technique.
Vipassana is actually just a meditative technique.
That's been very successful in America for obvious reasons.
But then there's been a second wave, which is these guys, [unclear: "Ajahn, Amar, Ajahn Tumaito"].
These are Westerners taking the full monk's ordination, maintaining that, living by all those many, many rules.
Like we've had [unclear: "Ajahn, Bhikkhu, Ajahn Jeff, Bhikkhu Tanasaro"] in Bellingham several times.
When he comes, they have all these extra arrangements to make, because he can't be in a room alone with a woman.
He can't handle money.
There's lots of things he can't do.
He can't feed himself.
He has to put food in his bowl.
He has to eat before noon.
And it's not even permitted for him to remind you about that either.
He just has to show up and trust that people will take care of him.
In his case, entering this culture, trust that they have enough background to know.
Because you could starve, right?
What's wonderful about this is that these guys are living this protected lifestyle of monks, so they get to practice a lot.
They can't have day jobs.
It's not allowed for them to have day jobs.
So it means there can't be very many of them, and they have to have somehow a community that's supporting them.
They're actually pretty expensive, it turns out.
Cindy Madigan, who's a bookkeeper and a Bipassan student here, went down to this guy's monastery called Abhya Giri.
She helped in the office or something like that, and that was one of the things she reported to me: monks are really expensive, actually.
I don't know if she had a dollar figure, but it takes a pretty good sized community to support a couple of monks.
They're bringing in a very deep sense of these teachings and, I think, in a beautiful way reinterpreting them in a very understandable way, so that you don't all have to be monks.
Anyway, a little background there.
This talk was called The Place of Non-Abiding.
It's really important for our practice, too.
Ajahn Amara said:
*You can't change their names.
You have to go by your Buddhist name.
Anyway, one of the topics that Ajahn Shah most liked to emphasize was the principle of non-abiding.

During the brief two years that I was with him in Thailand, he spoke about it many times and in various ways he tried to convey that non-abiding was the essence of the path, the basis of peace and a doorway into the world of freedom.*
So yeah, I guess Amara practiced under Ajahn Shah, who was still alive, for under three years, but Ajahn Sumedho practiced with him for many years.
He was a little older.
*During the summer of 1981, Ajahn Shah gave a very significant teaching to Ajahn Sumedho on the liberating quality of non-abiding.
Ajahn Sumedho had been in England for a few years, setting up a monastery, and later arrived from Thailand.
Even though Ajahn Shah could read and write, he rarely did.*
Ajahn Shah liked to pretty much meditate and talk to people about Dharma.
That's all he did all day.
He rarely did read or write.
In fact, he hardly wrote anything, and he never wrote letters.
*The message began with a note from a fellow Western monk.
It said, "Well Ajahn Sumedho, you are not going to believe this. [unclear: "A long court"] decided, he wanted to write you a letter, so he asked me to take this dictation."
The message from Ajahn Shah was very brief, and this is what it said:*
*Whenever you have feelings of love or hate for anything whatsoever, these will be your aids and partners in building parami, prajna, wisdom, building wisdom.
The Buddha Dharma is not to be found in moving forwards, nor in moving backwards, nor in standing still.
This Sumedho is your place of non-abiding.*
So think about this relative to our ceremonies too.
Whenever you have a feeling of love or hate for anything whatsoever, these are your aids and partners in building wisdom.
So love and hate are partners.
The Buddha Dharma is not to be found in moving forwards, nor in moving backwards, nor in standing still.
This Sumedho is your place of non-abiding.
Amara says:
*Thinking about this still gives me goosebumps.
A few weeks later Ajahn Shah had a stroke and became unable to speak, walk, or move.
So his verbal teaching career was over.
This letter contained his final instructions.
Ajahn Shah was well aware of all the tasks and difficulties involved in establishing a monastery, having done this many times.*
And that's what Sumedho was doing.
That's what we did here in our own small way, and we found it to be pretty stressful, wonderful, amazing, and stressful.
So yeah, you got some instructions from your teacher, and he hardly ever gives you instructions.
You'd probably be like, oh good, I need help.
*So you would think that he would have offered advice along the lines of, don't do this, do that, always remember this, but no, none of that.
That was not Ajahn Shah's way.
He simply said, the Buddha Dharma is not to be found in moving forwards, nor moving backwards, nor in standing still.*
So there's nowhere to stand.

*At his monastery in Thailand, Ajahn Shah would sit on a wicker bench in an open area underneath his hut and receive visitors from 10 o'clock in the morning until late at night, every day, sometimes until two or three in the morning.
Amongst the many ways in which he would convey the teachings, Ajahn Shah sometimes liked to test and tease his visitors.
He would put various conundrums out to them, queries or puzzles designed to frustrate and break through the limitations of the conditioned mind.
He would ask questions such as, is this stick long or short?
Or, where did you come from and where are you going?*
Which is a classic Zen question.
*Or as here, if you can't go forwards and you can't go back and you can't stand still, where do you go?
And when he'd put forth these questions, he'd have a look on his face like a cobra.*
I'll show it, a cobra.
Intent, I guess, very intent.
*Some of the more courageous responders would try a reasonable answer.
Go to one side?
No, you can't do that either.
Up or down?
And he would just keep pushing people as they struggled to come up with a right answer.
The more creative and clever they got, the more he would make them squirm.
No, no, no, that's not it.
Ajahn Shah would try to push his inquirers up against the limitations of the conditioned mind in hopes of opening up some space for the unconditioned to shine through.

The principle of non-abiding is exceedingly frustrating to the conceptual thinking mind, because that mind has built into it such an edifice of me and you out of here and there, past and future, this and that.*
And if you think about that, it's completely embedded in language, right?
Because if you can say something is this, what you're saying is it's not that.
But what if it's neither this nor that?
And it's not this nor that, right?
Where do you have left?
*As long as we conceive reality in terms of self and time, in terms of self and time, and from the point of view of a me who is some place*
and can go to some other place, then we are not realizing that going forwards, going backwards, and standing still are entirely dependent upon the relative truths of self, locality, and time.
In terms of physical reality, there is a coming and going, but there's also that place of transcendence where there is no coming and going.
Think about it.
Where can we really go?
Do you really go anywhere?
Wherever you go, you're always here, right?
To resolve the question, where can you go, we have to let go: let go of the self, let go of time, let go of place.
In that abandonment of self, time, and place, all questions are resolved.
So that's the kind of introduction.
There are two teachings from the Buddha, so I'll just do a little more.
I'll continue this another time.
This is really important, actually, non-abiding.
The principle of non-abiding is also contained within the ancient Theravada teachings.
It wasn't just Ajahn Chah's personal insight or the legacy of some stray Nyingmapa Lama who wandered over the mountains and fetched up in northeast Thailand 100 years ago.
Right in the Pali Canon, the Buddha points directly to this.
In the Udana, which is the collection of inspired utterances of the Buddha, he says,
*There is that sphere of being where there is no earth, no water, no fire, no wind,* which are the four elements that constitute material reality.
So there's a sphere of being where there's no material reality.
*No experience of infinity of space, of infinity of consciousness, of no thingness, or also a place of no non-conceptual reality.
Here...*
I'm sorry, I interrupted myself.
I'm starting over.

*There's a sphere of being where there's no earth, no water, no fire, nor wind, where there's no experience of infinity of space, of infinity of consciousness, of no thingness, or even of neither perception nor non-perception.
Here there is neither this world nor another world, neither sun nor moon.
This sphere of being I call neither a coming, nor a going, nor a staying still, neither a dying, nor a reappearance or birth.
It has no basis, no evolution, and no support.
It is the end of dukkha, the end of suffering.*
So, a sphere of being transcending all these sort of markers, which is also the end of suffering.
Amaro goes on.
*Rigpa,* which is a Tibetan word, so it's a response to the Tibetan guy.
*Non-dual awareness is the direct knowing of this.
Direct knowing of this.
It's a quality of mind that knows while abiding nowhere.
A quality of mind that knows while abiding nowhere.*
So you could say just knowing, or just knowing this.
So, knowing without an object that you're knowing.
Another teaching from the same collection recounts the story of a wanderer named Bahiya.
He stopped the Buddha on the street in Savatthi and said, *but venerable sir, you are the Samana Gautama.
Your dharma is famous throughout the land.
Please teach me that I may understand the truth.* The Buddha replied, *we are on our alms round now, Bahiya.
This is not the right time.* Bahiya said, *life is uncertain, venerable sir.
We must know when we're going to die.
Please teach me the dharma.* This dialogue repeats itself three times.
Three times over the Buddha says the same thing: it's not a good time.
And three times Bahiya repeats the same question.
Finally the Buddha says, this is like a cute thing that they had in all the [unclear: "mini sutras"].
You've got to ask three times.
And then maybe he'll answer.
And then he says, *when a Buddha has been pressed three times, he has to answer.
Listen carefully, Bahiya, and attend to what I have to say.* So he said,
*In the seen, like the seen with your eyes, what you see, S-E-E-N, in the seen, there is only the seen.
In the heard, there is only the heard.
In the sensed, there is only the sensed.
In the cognized, there is only the cognized.
Thus should you see that indeed there is no thing here.
This, Bahiya, is how you should train.*
So just see, just listen.
And even just think, just cognize what you're cognizing.
*Since, Bahiya, this is for you.
In the seen, only the seen.
In the heard, only the heard.
In the sensed, only the sensed.
In the cognized, only the cognized.
And you see that there is no thing here.
You will therefore see that indeed there is no thing there.
As you see that there is no thing there, you will see that you are therefore located neither in this world of this, nor in the world of that, nor in any place betwixt the two.
This alone is the end of suffering.*
So it's all playing with duality, right, with our limited way of interpreting the world with cognition, right, with concept.
It's got to be this or that.
It's got to be this or that.
And in that sort of engine of this, that, this, that, like, don't like, right, is suffering.
So the Buddha is saying there's another approach here besides this and that.
*Upon hearing these words, Bahiya was immediately enlightened.*
Here's the punchline.
*Moments later he was killed by a runaway cow.* So he was right.
Life is uncertain.
Let's practice the way immediately.
You know, one doesn't know, do these things really happen because of the teaching story?
Some of both, you know.
*And later, Bahiya was awarded the title of the disciple who understood the teaching most quickly.* Yeah, just in time.
Just in time.
So let's see.
I can't read this whole thing.
I'm just trying to think how much to read and how much to kind of leave it in some place where we have something we can do with all this stuff.
So I just, like, that was kind of interesting.
I wonder what he was talking about.
What does it mean to say, this is Amaro again, *what does it mean to say that there is no thing there?
It is talking about the realm of the object.
It implies that we recognize that the seen is merely the seen.* That's it.
So this week we can work with this.

This is a practice of, and you can practice this week, taking some time when you're in between things or during formal practice time, settling down, stilling the body, breathing, and seeing if you can allow perception to be much more bare, much more simple than it usually is.
And this only really happens when the mind is quiet.
And awareness of breathing is helpful too, because there's a sort of calming, quieting from the breathing.
So that when you hear something while you're sitting there, can you allow that to be just the sensation of hearing?
Just the heard.
Not, oh, a car's going by.
Or, oh, I forgot to take out the trash, you hear the garbage truck, right?
In my case it's my car.
And not conceptual elaboration, not judgment, not categorization, and even quieter than that, even below that, not even like, I like this sound, I don't like this sound.
So that you can practice this in regards to certain circumstances, next to a construction site or in the wonderful woods, same thing.
So in the heard, just the heard.
And the same with vision.
If you could stand quietly, and it is easier in nature, I think, but this is possible anywhere, on the sidewalk, and just settle the mind, actually open the eyes.
We have a way that the eyes are always sort of half open, because we don't want to take in too much.
Really open the eyes, and just let vision come in.
You know, releasing yourself as best you can from that whole sort of cognitive, self-based, evaluative judgment trip that we run at high speed every second.
So what they're saying is, the seeds of liberation are actually right there, right in, sort of embedded in actual perception.
So that's it, he says.
*The seen is merely the seen.

There are forms, shapes and colors and so forth, but there is no thing there.* So that's why it's operative: it's our creation of separation through this sort of rigidification of objects that we generate, the surfaces that can whack into us, right?
And grind us, you know, get under our skin.

It's because we believe that the annoying coworker is an annoying coworker, you know, and is someone other than you, and someone who should be in a different way, and you shouldn't say that, you know.
This huge stuff is going on, that we're not just perceiving the heard when she speaks.
There's no, so as you realize this, you see that there are forms, shapes and colors, you know, there's qualities to things.
Things do have qualities.
It's not saying that there's no qualities to things, or even no things, but there are no things.
There's no thing there, as a separate existent reality.
No real substance, no solidity, and no self-existent reality.
All there is is the quality of experience itself.
No more, and no less.
There's just seeing, hearing, feeling, sensing, cognizing, and the mind naming.
And the mind naming it all, as just another experience.
The space of the [unclear: "dharmahala"], Ajahn Amaro's voice, my voice, here is a thought, am I understanding this?
Now another thought, am I not understanding this?
He says.
So in other words, to kind of roll back the process to just our actual lived experience, you know, our actual lived experience.
What's actually happening now?
That I'm living my life and doing all these things and I'm stressed out and this and that is an additional sort of construct.
And all that's actually happening now is just these six things.
Just the five senses and the mind, cognizing thought, that's all that's actually happening.
And then we can work with that skillfully and have less suffering, or unskillfully and have more.
And as this insight matures, not only do we realize that there is no thing out there, but we also realize that there's no solid thing in here.
No independent and fixed entity that is the experiencer.
This is talking about the realm of the subject.
And this practice of non-abiding is a practice of emptying out the objective and subjective domains.
And really seeing that both the object and the subject are intrinsically empty.
If we can see that both the subjective and objective are empty, and if there's no real in here or out there, where could the feeling of I-ness and me-ness and my-ness locate itself?
And where could it be?

As the Buddha said to Bahiya, *you will not be able to find yourself either in the world of this,* the subject, *or the world of that,* the object, *or anywhere in between the two.* Could we continue to this?
Does that make any sense whatsoever?
Non-sensical sort of sense.
But you can practice with this.
And little by little, you know, it's not like one sort of jumps into these things, but maybe you fall into it sometimes.
You can't make these things happen exactly.
And I'm not claiming any [unclear: "business mastery"] of all this either, so don't go projecting on me.
Or anybody.
These guys are wearing their little things.
They do not claim to be masters of this either.

But by supporting each other and practicing steadily, we really can reduce this quality of mind, this tendency of mind to objectify, rigidify, react to, believe in the solidness of the external world and the internal world.
That's really important, the internal world.
We really think that I'm stuck in my tendencies, stuck in my personality and my problems.
I'm this kind of person.
I don't like that kind of person.
But that's all made up.
It's powerful.
It's permanent, right?
It keeps arising.
But what they're saying is, it's not permanent.
It just keeps arising and going away and arising and going away.
It's not there all the time.
It doesn't actually exist in that way.

And the sort of most basic and fundamental way to do that is simply, is not sort of thinking yourself out of it, but simply directly and experientially returning to the present moment, to what's actually happening now.
All that elaborative stuff loses some of its grip.
If you're really just breathing, really just hearing, you can see: I was stressed out ten minutes ago.
I might be stressed out ten minutes from now, but at the moment I'm actually just breathing.
It's not actually happening right now.
But then you have to do all this with a very patient and gentle touch so you don't sort of get mad at yourself when ten minutes later it's all back, right?
Because what a silly thing that would be to think, okay, if I'm not permanently messed up, maybe I could be permanently not messed up.
It's the same thing.
It's the same thing.
It's the same sort of believing in sort of a fixedness that doesn't actually exist.
